idiom_name: maker-checker rows under ActiveRecord with_lock + an explicit policy object at the service boundary
implementation_notes: Rails provides the atomicity primitive and leaves the rule to you: ActiveRecord with_lock wraps the block in a transaction, reloads the record with a row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) and yields with it locked, which is exactly what a maker-checker transition needs - compare approver != initiated_by, flip the state and write the actor in one critical section. Authorization is not in the standard library: Pundit/CanCanCan, or hand-rolled policy objects, decide who may invoke the release action, and the separation predicate is the extra condition those policies do not express for you. What replaces the classic structure is the locked workflow row plus a policy object owned by a service; keep both out of the controller so the check cannot be skipped by a second entry point.
code_sketch:
class ReleasePayment
  def call(payment_id, approver)
    Payment.transaction do
      p = Payment.lock.find(payment_id)              # SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
      raise NotAuthorized, 'maker cannot approve' if p.initiated_by_id == approver.id
      raise Conflict, p.status unless p.pending?
      p.update!(status: :approved, approved_by: approver)
    end
  end
end
pitfalls: The lock only helps when every write path uses it: an admin console or update_column outside with_lock reopens the race and can also skip the distinctness check.
Mass assignment can set approved_by/status directly (permit lists, update(params)); keep those attributes out of permitted parameters and enforce the state machine on the model.
A validation or callback that consults ambient state (Current.user, session) makes the invariant depend on the caller's context and silently passes in background jobs and console sessions.
